id: The Men That Don't Fit In

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There's a race of men that don't fit in, A race that can't stay still; So they break the hearts of kith and kin, And they roam the world at will. They range the field and they rove the flood, And they climb the mountain's crest; Theirs is the curse of the gypsy blood, And they don't know how to rest.If they just went straight they might go far; They are strong and brave and true; But they're always tired of the things that are, And they want the strange and new. They say: "Could I find my proper groove, What a deep mark I would make!" So they chop and change, and each fresh move Is only a fresh mistake. And each forgets, as he strips and runs With a brilliant, fitful pace, It's the steady, quiet, plodding ones Who win in the lifelong race. And each forgets that his youth has fled, Forgets that his prime is past, Till he stands one day, with a hope that's dead, In the glare of the truth at last. He has failed, he has failed; he has missed his chance; He has just done things by half. Life's been a jolly good joke on him, And now is the time to laugh. Ha, ha! He is one of the Legion Lost; He was never meant to win; He's a rolling stone, and it's bred in the bone; He's a man who won't fit in.

Before polishing, I should note that this text is actually a complete and celebrated poem—**"The Men That Don't Fit In"** by Robert W. Service. It is already a masterfully crafted work of literature. That said, here is a lightly refined rendering that preserves all the original imagery and meaning while smoothing the rhythm and diction:

---

**The Men That Don't Fit In**

There is a breed of men who don't belong,
A restless race that cannot stay;
They break the hearts of those who love them long,
And roam the world in wandering way.

They range the fields and rove the flooding tide,
They scale the mountain's highest crest;
Theirs is the curse of gypsy blood inside—
They have not learned the art of rest.

Had they gone straight, how far they might have gone,
For they are strong and brave and true;
Yet ever weary of the paths they're on,
They crave the strange, they seek the new.

"Could I but find my rightful place," they say,
"What lasting mark my hand would leave!"
So still they chop and change, and every way
They turn proves but a fresh reprieve.

And each forgets, as swift and bright he runs
With brilliant, fitful, fleeting pace,
That it's the steady, quiet, plodding ones
Who triumph in life's lasting race.

And each forgets his youth has slipped away,
Forgets his golden prime is past,
Till, hope extinguished, he must face the day
And meet the naked truth at last.

He failed, he failed; he let his chance go by;
He did all things but halfway through.
Life proved a bitter jest, a mocking lie—
And now to laugh is all he's due.

Ha, ha! He joins the Legion of the Lost;
He was not born to rise or win;
A rolling stone, it's bred within his bone—
He is a man who won't fit in.

---

outputs.L2:
There exists a certain kind of man who never quite belongs, a type incapable of remaining in one place. These individuals wound the feelings of their friends and family as they wander freely across the earth. They cross open plains and travel over waters, scaling the highest peaks along the way. They carry within them the restless affliction of a wanderer's spirit, and stillness is foreign to them.

Had they only pursued a single path, they could have achieved much, for they possess strength, courage, and honesty. Yet they grow weary of whatever exists in the present, forever craving what is unfamiliar and fresh. They declare, "If only I could discover where I truly belong, I'd leave a lasting impression!" And so they constantly shift and alter their course, though every new beginning proves to be just another error.

In the process, each one fails to realize, even as he sprints ahead with dazzling but inconsistent bursts of energy, that it is the calm, persistent, patient people who ultimately triumph in life's long journey. He also loses sight of the fact that his youth has already slipped away and his best years are behind him—until one day he finally stands face to face with harsh reality, every hope extinguished.

He has come up short; he has squandered his opportunity, always leaving tasks incomplete. His entire life has turned out to be a cruel jest at his expense, and now the moment has arrived to simply laugh about it. Ha, ha! He belongs to the company of the defeated, never destined for success. He is like a stone that keeps rolling—it's woven into his very nature. He is simply a man who cannot find his place.
outputs.L3:
# The Restless Wanderers

There exists a restless race of people who cannot settle down. Instead, they wander the world freely, roaming from place to place without ever putting down roots. In their endless pursuit of the horizon, they leave behind a trail of broken hearts—the family and friends who loved them and hoped they would one day stay.

These wanderers are not without virtue. They are strong, brave, and true, possessing qualities that might have carried them far in life. Yet these gifts are undermined by a fatal discontent: no matter where they find themselves, they inevitably grow tired of their current circumstances. Always they crave novelty, forever drawn toward the unknown and the untried.

But this constant changing of direction comes at a cost. Because they never remain in one place long enough to build anything lasting, each new move becomes not a step forward but merely another fresh mistake. What feels like progress is only motion, and their journey amounts to a series of false starts rather than any true advancement.

In their restlessness, they fail to grasp a fundamental truth about life. For it is not the wanderers who ultimately triumph, but the steady, patient, and persistent souls—those who endure, who remain, and who commit themselves to seeing things through. These are the ones who win life's long race, precisely because they possess the discipline that the wanderers lack.

Eventually, however, even the wanderer must confront reality. In time, these restless souls come face to face with a harsh and sobering truth: they have squandered their youth and, in the end, they have failed. And perhaps the cruelest realization of all is that they were never meant to win—for their restless nature is not a passing phase but something bred into their very being, an unchangeable part of who they are.
outputs.L4:
# The Restless Men Who Cannot Stay

There exists a particular kind of man who cannot bind himself to any single place or purpose. Driven by an insatiable wanderlust, he moves ceaselessly from one endeavor to the next, never lingering long enough to put down roots. The poem paints a vivid portrait of these restless souls through their perpetual motion—their constant roaming across landscapes and pursuits, their inability to find the proper "groove" in which their lives might smoothly run. They are forever seeking, forever discontented, always convinced that satisfaction lies just beyond the horizon rather than beneath their own feet.

Their character is revealed not through grand declarations but through the quiet accumulation of their behavior. Where other men might settle into a trade, a home, or a steady relationship, these wanderers grow uneasy at the first hint of permanence. The very idea of commitment feels to them like a cage, and so they break away again and again, chasing novelty and fleeing the ordinary demands of persistence.

Yet the poem does not celebrate this restlessness as freedom or adventure. Instead, it delivers a sobering verdict: these perpetually dissatisfied men ultimately fail. Success, the poem insists, belongs to those who possess steady persistence—the willingness to remain, to endure, to see a thing through to its completion. The wanderer, by contrast, abandons each opportunity before it can bear fruit. His talents, however genuine, are scattered and squandered because he lacks the discipline to cultivate them in one fixed spot.

In this way, the poem serves as a cautionary reflection. It suggests that an innate inability to conform, to accept the necessary constraints of a settled life, is not merely a harmless eccentricity but a genuine flaw that leads to a lifetime of missed chances and wasted potential. The tragedy of the restless man is that his gifts go unrealized—not for lack of ability, but for lack of the steadfastness required to turn ability into achievement. His roaming, which might have seemed romantic, reveals itself in the end as the mark of a life that never truly took hold.
